summary: Extends the ISATAP interface, which normally carries IPv6 packets over an IPv4 network using automatic tunneling, so that it can also encapsulate and carry IPv4 packets. The original ISATAP specifications made no provision for this. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: ISATAP is a tunnel that normally carries one kind of message. This update lets the same tunnel carry the older kind of message too.

questions: how can isatap carry ipv4 packets
subtitle: Extending ISATAP to carry both IPv6 and IPv4 packets over IPv4 networks.

tldr.problem: ISATAP was designed to carry only IPv6 packets over IPv4 networks. This limits its use in scenarios where nodes need to exchange IPv4 packets through an IPv4-based site.
tldr.mechanism: The specification extends ISATAP to also perform automatic IPv4-in-IPv4 encapsulation, mirroring its existing IPv6 capabilities. Nodes assign themselves IPv4 addresses from a site-scoped prefix and map neighbor addresses through configured lookup methods.
tldr.outcome: ISATAP can now tunnel both IPv4 and IPv6 across IPv4 networks, broadening its applicability to enterprise networks and transition scenarios.

today: RFC 5579 is an Informational document that extends [RFC5214]. It has not been obsoleted and defines the standard method for transmitting IPv4 packets over ISATAP interfaces when such functionality is needed.

sections.title: Overview and Motivation
sections.content:
ISATAP (Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol) [RFC5214] specifies a method for transmitting IPv6 packets over IPv4 networks using automatic encapsulation. Nodes within a connected IPv4 routing topology (called a site) can configure IPv6 addresses and communicate over a virtual IPv6 overlay.

The original ISATAP specification provided no mechanism for transmitting IPv4 packets through ISATAP interfaces. This document extends ISATAP to support IPv4-in-IPv4 encapsulation, allowing nodes to send IPv4 packets through the same tunnel infrastructure. This enables ISATAP to serve broader enterprise network scenarios, such as the RANGER and VET proposals.
sections.plainLanguage: ISATAP lets computers send messages through a tunnel over regular IPv4 networks. At first it only handled one type of message format, but this explains how to make it handle an older format too.

sections.title: ISATAP Interface Model
sections.content:
ISATAP interfaces span a region within a connected IPv4 routing topology as a single IPv6 hop. Border nodes with ISATAP interfaces forward packets across the site in one hop, while ordinary IPv4 routers between them decrement the IPv4 Time To Live (TTL). This means border nodes appear as single-hop neighbors to each other, even if separated by many IPv4 hops.

The same interface model applies to IPv4 operation: the ISATAP interface spans the same underlying IPv4 site for both IPv6-in-IPv4 and IPv4-in-IPv4 encapsulation. The MTU considerations are identical to those in [RFC4213].
sections.plainLanguage: An ISATAP interface acts like a one-hop bridge across an IPv4 network, even when the two endpoints are far apart. This works the same way for both IPv6 and IPv4 messages.

sections.title: IPv4 Addressing and Route Configuration
sections.content:
For IPv4 operation, each ISATAP interface must be assigned a unique Layer 3 address (L3ADDR) from an IPv4 prefix for the site. This address is used for next-hop determination and may also serve as the source address for packets originating from the ISATAP interface itself.

When the ISATAP site must be distinguished from other sites, L3ADDR is taken from a public IPv4 prefix. Otherwise, it may be taken from a link-local prefix such as 169.254/16 [RFC3927], allocated using DHCP [RFC2131], or configured manually.

IPv4 Forwarding Information Base (FIB) entries are configured over ISATAP interfaces through administrative or dynamic mechanisms, just as with any IPv4 interface. Next-hop addresses in these entries correspond to the L3ADDR of neighboring ISATAP interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint on an ISATAP tunnel gets its own address number so the other endpoints know where to send messages. This address can come from the site's address pool or from a temporary block.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Transmission
sections.content:
When IPv4 packets arrive at an ISATAP interface, the node first determines which outgoing ISATAP interface and next-hop L3ADDR to use by performing an IPv4 FIB lookup. The packet length is checked against the interface MTU. If the packet is larger than the MTU, the Don't Fragment flag is examined: if set, an ICMP fragmentation-needed message is returned; otherwise, the packet is fragmented.

After determining the next-hop L3ADDR, the node must map it to a Layer 2 address (L2ADDR), which is the IPv4 address of an underlying interface of the ISATAP neighbor. This mapping differs from IPv6 operation, where algorithmic mapping is possible; IPv4 mapping requires a site-wide convention, such as name service lookup or static mapping tables.

The packet is then encapsulated as specified in [RFC2003], with the underlying interface's IPv4 address as the outer source and the L2ADDR as the outer destination. The IP protocol field is set to 4 (IPv4-in-IPv4). The encapsulated packet is submitted to the IPv4 layer, which may fragment it further before transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: When sending an IPv4 message through ISATAP, the node wraps it in another IPv4 header with the recipient's real IPv4 address on the outside, then sends it as a normal IPv4 packet.

sections.title: Multicast and Recursive Encapsulation
sections.content:
For ISATAP interfaces deployed on sites that support IPv4 multicast, IPv4 multicast packets can be mapped to Organization-Local Scope multicast addresses. When an IPv4 packet with a multicast destination address is sent on an ISATAP interface, it is encapsulated and transmitted to a mapped multicast address taken from 239.193.0.0/16 or other expansion blocks, following the same approach used in 6over4 [RFC2529].

To avoid routing loops, nodes must carefully manage their IPv4 FIB table entries to prevent recursive encapsulations. This is a critical consideration during implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: ISATAP can also handle group messages sent to many recipients at once. Special care is needed to make sure messages do not get wrapped twice by mistake.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The security considerations for IPv4 transmission over ISATAP are the same as those for IP Encapsulation within IP [RFC2003], since the mechanism uses the same IPv4-in-IPv4 encapsulation. ISATAP inherits its security model from [RFC5214] and 6over4 [RFC2529], except that IPv4-in-IPv4 encapsulation (protocol 4) is used instead of IPv6-in-IPv4 encapsulation (protocol 41).

Tunnel security considerations for IPv4-in-IPv4 encapsulation over ISATAP are discussed in related work on tunnel security. Implementers should be aware that IP-in-IP tunnels can be subject to spoofing attacks if source address filtering is not properly applied.
sections.plainLanguage: Wrapping messages inside other messages creates the same security risks as other tunneling methods. Sites using ISATAP should apply the same protections they would use for other IPv4 tunnels.
